new_statements.rule_in_words: Heiltsuk proper is a two-tone (high/low) language with tonal minimal pairs, but tone placement is largely rule-governed and culminative-like: at most three high tones per word (rule 1), a word-initial doubleton (VV) must carry a high tone (3b), and among singleton full vowels the first one takes high tone while later ones are low (6b); glottalized vowels are always low; proclitics are always low; a residue of suffix/enclitic allomorphs carries lexical (unpredictable) high tone. Rath 1974 adds that accent (stress) and length are 'linked with pitch and predictable' (accent accompanying the first high-pitched vowel for his main consultant). The Oowekyala variety has no tone but a predictable accent on the first full vowel /V/ of the phonemic word (second /V/ when the first derives from schwa). Wilson 1987 independently: Heiltsuq H tone sits where common Wakashan puts primary stress (first heavy syllable) and is synchronically phonemic.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress for Heiltsuk or Oowekyala in Rath 1974/1985. Wilson 1987 p.322 states only for common Wakashan (not Heiltsuq) 'primary stress to the first heavy syllable of a word, with alternating secondary stress thereafter'.
new_statements.exceptions: Rath 1985: vocatives, interjections, borrowings, songs, onomatopoeia and full root reduplications exempt from doubleton rule 3b; singletons deriving from schwa are low unless suffix-final and word-final or before a T/R-initial enclitic (6a, 6a-1); lexical high tone in certain suffix/enclitic allomorphs (e.g. /-ba/ 'point, end', enclitic allomorph of -Rxo) and morphophonemically caused unpredictable high tones (pp.318-320). Oowekyala: when the first /V/ derives morphophonemically from schwa and is followed by [a garbled segment], 'the second /V/ of the phonemic word bears accent' (p.316). Rath 1974 3.2.2: place of accent within a pitch contour 'appears to be a matter of dialect' (speaker Freeman vs Campbell).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'phonemic word' = lexical word plus clitics (Rath 1985 rule 1 'lexical or combined with clitics'; proclitics always low-toned, enclitics covered by the rules). Data are elicited citation forms (Rath 1974 notes pitch 'starting-point' varies between elicited words). The Glottolog languoid heil1246 covers both Heiltsuk (tonal) and Oowekyala (non-tonal, initial-full-vowel accent); a catalog entry must say which variety it codes.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog heil1246 'Heiltsuk-Oowekyala' lumps two prosodically different varieties. Rath 1974/1985 and Wilson 1987 describe Heiltsuk proper (Bella Bella/Waglisla and Klemtu speech; Glottolog dialect bell1263 'Bella Bella' / Haíɫzaqvḷa), which is tonal (high vs low, largely predictable, first-singleton-high). The Oowekyala variety of Rivers Inlet (Glottolog dialect oowe1239) is described in the same Rath 1985 paper (p.315-316) and in Rath 1992 fn.5 / Wilson 1987 p.321 as NON-tonal with predictable accent on the first full vowel of the phonemic word. A catalog row should code the two separately or state which one it represents.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (Heiltsuk tonal, high vs low; Oowekyala accent instead of tone, predictable): agrees on kind. Adds the explicit Oowekyala placement rule (first vocalic plain resonant, else the second of two adjacent ones) and the Heiltsuk distributional limits (max three H, no H on contiguous resonants, glottalized resonants toneless-low). One nuance: this 1980 text calls the He tones 'phonologically unpredictable' (lexical), whereas Rath 1985 (the catalog source, later analysis) finds most of them predictable from phonotactic and morphophonemic parameters; not a contradiction of type or placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Heiltsuk (Bella Bella/Klemtu): every vocalic plain resonant (vowel or syllabic m n l) carries lexical high or low tone; tone is phonologically unpredictable (minimal pairs) but constrained: at most three high tones per word (then the last two in the configuration R R-consonantal R), never two high tones on contiguous resonants, glottalized vocalic resonants always low. Oowekyala (Rivers Inlet): no tone but a predictable stress accent: stress on the first vocalic plain resonant of the word, or on the second when the first is immediately followed by another vocalic plain resonant; a grave accent is written only in the few words where stress is not predictable by these two rules; glottalized vocalic resonants are never stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress for Heiltsuk or Oowekyala (secondary stress is described only for Haisla, sec. 3.3 p.28: 'there is often secondary stress on preceding occurrences of R/a').
new_statements.exceptions: He: vocatives, exclamations and (foreign?) proper names may exceed three high tones; low tone before a high tone often sounds mid. Oo: stress marked with a grave in the few unpredictable words (e.g. k'wuaqà 'to split wood roughly'); the second of two adjacent resonants counts as stressed as long as it is not less loud than the first; orthographic m n l i u a followed by the glottal sign are glottalized resonants and always unstressed.
new_statements.identity_note: heil1246 covers Heiltsuk proper (Bella Bella and Klemtu, incl. the 'Xíxís of Klemtu) and Oowekyala (Rivers Inlet). Lincoln & Rath 1980 treat them together as 'Heiltsuk-Oowekyala' but state that He has tone and Oo has stress accent; Rath 1981 describes Bella Bella/Klemtu Heiltsuk only (consultants from Bella Bella and Klemtu; one Oowekyala-speaking consultant used for cross-checking).

new_statements.quote: [p.5] Henceforward, both in the orthography and in phonetic transcriptions, an acute (´) over a vowel indicates high tone whereas its absence indicates low tone. Variation in the pitch level of the high and the low tone is ignored. [p.7] As the chart of vowels shows, glottalized vowels occur with low tone exclusively. [p.41] In a series of plain vowels only one can have high tone, the other(s) necessarily having low tone. [p.44] A sequence of the type /VRVC/ ... may exhibit the following tone configurations when preceded by any obstruent ...: low-low, high-low, high-high. new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the catalog record's classification tonal (Heiltsuk high vs low tone, as in Rath 1985 and Kortlandt 1975); silent on stress/accent placement and on predictability beyond phonotactic tone configurations, so it neither adds a placement rule nor contradicts Rath 1985's morphophonemic predictability claim. The bibliography tag 'likely states stress' is not borne out: the cited chapters state tone marking and tone distribution only.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Heiltsuk is described with two phonemic tones, high (acute) and low (unmarked), written lexically on every vowel/vocalic resonant of every dictionary entry; the grammatical introduction gives distributional constraints on tone (glottalized vowels always low; only one high tone in a plain-vowel series; permitted tone configurations over /VRVC/; low-high only in vocatives, exclamations and certain 'out of' allomorphs) and marks suffix allomorphs as high-only, low-only or either (p.69), but states no stress or accent rule and has no prosody section. Nothing on Oowekyala accent (the book covers Bella Bella and Klemtu Heiltsuk).
new_statements.exceptions: Vocatives, exclamations and the 'out of the house / out of open space / out of enclosed space' allomorphs /uwls, uwis, uwit/ allow the otherwise excluded low-high configuration (p.49-50); loanwords (e.g. sgvuél from English 'school') break the vowel-distribution rules (p.49).

tone_statements.quote: A HE vocalic plain resonant that is neither preceded nor followed by another one has either high tone indicated by an acute, or low tone indicated by its absence, cf. HE /k̓ʷás/ 'mussel' versus HE /k̓ʷas/ 'sit on the ground outside'. The other isolects have accent instead. ... A series of vocalic plain resonants has only one tone or accent; the placement of the tone or accent in the series is not distinctive. ... The HE tones are often predictable morphophonemically but the rules are too many to be explained in this paper and the reader has to be referred to Rath (1985).
tone_statements.summary: High vs low tone on plain vocalic resonants, from author's fieldwork (minimal pair given); at least 25 tone-marked HE forms; a morphophoneme 'imparts high tone'; sister isolects have accent, not tone.

tone_statements.citation: Kortlandt, Frederik H.H. 1975. Tones in Wakashan. Linguistics 13(146): 31-34.
tone_statements.quote: 3. The most salient feature of Heiltsuk phonetics is the presence of phonemic pitch. Vowels and syllabic resonants are high (´) or low (`). Stress is automatic and falls on the first high-pitched syllable of a word, if any. The large majority of words contain at least one high-pitched syllable, but this is not necessarily so ... The tone of a suffix depends not only on the suffix itself but also on the preceding stem, and, what is more, not only on the pitch contour of the preceding stem.
tone_statements.summary: Two-way high/low pitch contrast from the author's 1972 Klemtu fieldwork (4000+ words); c. 170 tone-marked forms; suffix tone classes, lowering before future -λ-; Rivers Inlet dialect lacks tone.

sources.note: First published report of Heiltsuk phonemic tone (cited as such by Rath 1985 and Wilson 1987); short primary statement with the original minimal pairs and suffix tone classes.

tone.quote: 3. The most salient feature of Heiltsuk phonetics is the presence of phonemic pitch. Vowels and syllabic resonants are high (´) or low (`). Stress is automatic and falls on the first high-pitched syllable of a word, if any. The large majority of words contain at least one high-pitched syllable, but this is not necessarily so ... The tone of a suffix depends not only on the suffix itself but also on the preceding stem, and, what is more, not only on the pitch contour of the preceding stem.
tone.summary: Two-way high/low pitch contrast from the author's 1972 Klemtu fieldwork (4000+ words); c. 170 tone-marked forms; suffix tone classes, lowering before future -λ-; Rivers Inlet dialect lacks tone.

sources.note: Per the Wikipedia paraphrase (secondhand, pp. 5-10, 40 cited): analyses Heiltsuk as a mixed tone-stress system. TBU = mora (full vowel, or schwa+plain resonant coda, or syllabic m n l; schwa in open syllable, schwa+glottalized resonant and glottalized syllabic resonants are non-moraic and never bear H). Default stress on the leftmost mora, realized as high pitch; a word with no mora has no high pitch (pk̓vs 'sasquatch' vs pk̓vsáx̌i); some function words (his, la) never high.
